interactions.label: In bronchial asthma, the late-phase response occurring 6–12 hours after allergen

params.question: In bronchial asthma, the late-phase response occurring 6–12 hours after allergen exposure is predominantly driven by:

answers.text: Mast cells releasing histamine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mast cell degranulation with histamine release characterises the early-phase response (within minutes of allergen exposure), not the late-phase response at 6–12 hours.

answers.text: Neutrophils and macrophages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutrophils and macrophages are the predominant inflammatory cells in COPD, not in the asthmatic late-phase response. This distinction is central to choosing the right drug class for each condition.

answers.text: Eosinophils recruited by cytokines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IL-5 drives eosinophil production and survival, while IL-4 and IL-13 promote IgE class-switching, sustaining the late-phase inflammatory cascade that leads to airway remodelling.

answers.text: Basophils producing IgE

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IgE is produced by B lymphocytes after class-switching driven by IL-4 and IL-13, not by basophils. The late-phase response is dominated by eosinophils flooding into the airway.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the biphasic inflammatory response: the early phase is driven by mast cell degranulation (minutes), while the late phase (6–12 hours) is dominated by eosinophils recruited by cytokines such as IL-5.
The biphasic asthma response is clinically important: the early phase is mast cell/histamine-mediated, while the late phase is eosinophil-dominated and drives chronic airway remodelling.

interactions.label: Why must long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABAs) never be prescribed as monotherapy

params.question: Why must long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABAs) never be prescribed as monotherapy in bronchial asthma?

answers.text: They cause rapid tachyphylaxis, losing bronchodilator effect within days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While some tolerance to beta-2 agonist effects can develop, this is not the primary safety concern. The critical issue is that LABA monotherapy has been linked to increased asthma-related mortality.

answers.text: They worsen airway remodelling by directly stimulating smooth muscle hypertrophy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LABAs do not cause smooth muscle hypertrophy. Airway remodelling is driven by chronic eosinophilic inflammation, which LABAs do not address — hence the need for concurrent inhaled corticosteroids.

answers.text: They are ineffective as bronchodilators unless combined with a corticosteroid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LABAs are effective bronchodilators on their own. The problem is not lack of efficacy but increased mortality when the underlying eosinophilic inflammation remains untreated.

answers.text: They have been associated with increased asthma-related deaths when used without inhaled corticosteroids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Clinical evidence showed higher asthma mortality with LABA monotherapy. LABAs relieve symptoms but do not address the underlying inflammation, masking worsening disease. Note: LABA monotherapy is acceptable in COPD.

overallFeedback.feedback: LABA monotherapy in asthma is linked to increased deaths because it relieves bronchoconstriction while leaving eosinophilic inflammation unchecked. Always combine with inhaled corticosteroids in asthma.
This is a critical safety rule: LABA + ICS is mandatory in asthma. In contrast, LABA monotherapy is acceptable in COPD, where the inflammatory mechanism and safety profile differ.

interactions.label: A patient with allergic rhinitis reports that cetirizine has relieved her sneezi

params.question: A patient with allergic rhinitis reports that cetirizine has relieved her sneezing and itching, but nasal congestion persists. What is the pharmacological explanation for this incomplete response?

answers.text: Nasal congestion is primarily mediated by alpha-adrenergic vascular pathways, not by histamine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Histamine acts mainly on nerve endings and secretory glands, driving sneezing, itching, and rhinorrhoea. Nasal congestion results from vascular engorgement controlled by alpha-adrenergic receptors, which antihistamines cannot address.

answers.text: Cetirizine is a weak H1 blocker that fails to reach adequate nasal mucosal concentrations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cetirizine is a potent second-generation H1-receptor antagonist with good bioavailability. The issue is not drug potency but the fact that congestion is mediated by a different receptor pathway altogether.

answers.text: Second-generation antihistamines lack the anti-inflammatory properties needed for decongestion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While anti-inflammatory effects vary among antihistamines, the real reason is that congestion is not histamine-mediated. Intranasal corticosteroids address congestion by reducing inflammation across all mediator pathways.

answers.text: Prolonged antihistamine use leads to histamine receptor upregulation in nasal blood vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Receptor upregulation with antihistamine use is not a recognised clinical phenomenon. Congestion persists because it is driven by alpha-adrenergic vascular pathways, not histamine receptors.

overallFeedback.feedback: Histamine drives sneezing, itching, and rhinorrhoea but plays only a minor role in nasal vascular congestion. Congestion is controlled by alpha-adrenergic pathways — that is why antihistamines alone leave it untreated.
This explains why intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective monotherapy for allergic rhinitis — they address all four cardinal symptoms including congestion, which antihistamines cannot.

interactions.label: A patient presents with a productive cough bringing up mucopurulent sputum follo

params.question: A patient presents with a productive cough bringing up mucopurulent sputum following a lower respiratory tract infection. Why would prescribing an antitussive be inappropriate in this situation?

answers.text: Antitussives are contraindicated in bacterial infections due to drug interactions with antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no significant interaction between antitussives and antibiotics. The issue is that suppressing the cough reflex in a productive cough impairs the body's mechanism for clearing infected secretions.

answers.text: Suppressing a productive cough impairs airway clearance of secretions that the body needs to expel

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When cough is productive, the reflex is protective — it clears mucus, pathogens, and debris from the airways. Suppressing it leads to retained secretions, which can worsen infection and impair recovery.

answers.text: Codeine-based antitussives are ineffective against infection-related cough because the reflex arc differs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Codeine suppresses cough regardless of aetiology by acting centrally on the medullary cough centre. The problem is not inefficacy but that suppression is actively harmful when secretions need to be cleared.

answers.text: Productive cough always resolves spontaneously and never requires any pharmacological intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Productive cough often does need treatment — but the correct approach is to facilitate secretion clearance using expectorants, mucolytics, hydration, and chest physiotherapy, not to suppress the reflex.

overallFeedback.feedback: In productive cough, the reflex is protective. Suppressing it retains secretions and can worsen the underlying condition. The correct approach is to aid clearance with expectorants, mucolytics, and adequate hydration.

The dry-versus-productive distinction is the single most important assessment in cough management: suppress only dry cough; facilitate clearance in productive cough; and always treat the underlying cause.

interactions.label: A 50-year-old non-smoking woman with a normal chest radiograph has had a persist

params.question: A 50-year-old non-smoking woman with a normal chest radiograph has had a persistent dry cough for ten weeks. She takes enalapril for hypertension. What is the most appropriate first step in managing her cough?

answers.text: Prescribe dextromethorphan for symptomatic cough suppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Symptomatic relief without addressing the underlying cause is not rational cough management. This patient has an identifiable and reversible drug-related cause that should be addressed first.

answers.text: Start empirical antibiotics for suspected atypical pneumonia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A normal chest radiograph and absence of systemic symptoms make atypical pneumonia unlikely. The clinical profile — chronic dry cough in a patient on an ACE inhibitor — points strongly to a drug-induced cause.

answers.text: Switch enalapril to an angiotensin receptor blocker and reassess after a few weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ACE inhibitor–induced cough is one of the three most common causes of chronic cough (>8 weeks) in non-smokers with a normal chest radiograph. Switching to an ARB typically resolves the cough within 1–4 weeks.

answers.text: Order high-resolution CT thorax to exclude interstitial lung disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Advanced imaging is not warranted as a first step when a clear drug-related cause is present. The rational approach is to address the most likely reversible cause first and investigate further only if the cough persists.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a non-smoker with a normal CXR and chronic dry cough on an ACE inhibitor, drug-induced cough is the most likely diagnosis. Switch to an ARB first; investigate further only if the cough persists after 1–4 weeks.

Rational cough management follows a structured algorithm: characterise the cough, identify the most likely cause, and treat the cause before adding symptomatic therapy. ACE inhibitor cough is a classic reversible cause.
